title: Eviction throttle causing intermittent latency spikes and stream-epoch reconciliation failures
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Summary:
We are observing intermittent token-level latency spikes and growing RSS on hosts serving continuous-batching workloads. Symptoms point to eviction throttling in the KV cache interplay with the allocator's cudaMallocAsync mempool: when the KV eviction process backs off under load, freed device memory is not being returned to the mempool fast enough and pinned staging buckets grow, leading to transient fragmentation and reclaim delays across CUDA streams.

Goals:
- Reproduce a minimal repro across our synthetic continuous-batching harness.
- Correlate eviction throttle events with allocator metrics (mempool free queue length, deferred-free backlog, stream-epoch drift).
- Propose and prototype mitigations: eviction hysteresis, targeted async free flushes, and a stream-epoch reconciliation pass that forces mempool trimming on safe boundaries.

Background / hypothesis:
1) The KV cache eviction throttle was recently tightened to avoid heavy eviction storms under peak throughput. That throttle keeps the eviction workqueue shallow. Under mixed sequence length traffic, the mempool sees many short-lived allocations followed by few larger pops; when eviction is throttled we end up with many freed allocations that are left in the per-stream deferred free lists rather than reclaimed to the global mempool quickly.
2) cudaMallocAsync's pooling semantics and our pinned host staging buckets combine to create a two-tier backlog: device-resident freed blocks remain associated with streams (or stashed in mempool arenas) until an epoch-sweep touches them. If the sweep cadence lags due to the throttle, fragmentation increases and subsequent large allocations suffer placement failures or fall back to expensive device-level OS allocs, causing token latency spikes.
3) The interaction is amplified by continuous batching windows where hot KV keys cause repeated cache churn on the same streams, preventing normal epoch progress.

Reproducer steps:
- Use continuous-batch harness: 512 concurrency, request lengths randomized between 64-2048 tokens, enable KV caching with TTL 30s, and eviction throttle tuned to 10 ops/sec. (See harness commit referenced below.)
- Run for 45 minutes and capture: /metrics/mempool_free_queue_length, /metrics/deferred_free_count_per_stream, /metrics/allocator_fallback_count, and per-token latency histograms.
- Expect to see deferred_free_count_per_stream drift upward prior to latency spikes, followed by mempool fallback events.

Telemetry & dashboards:
- Grafana panel: runtime/mempool/free_queue_length (linked), deferred-free per stream heatmap, allocator fallback counter by host, token p99 by route.

Proposed mitigations to prototype:
A) Eviction hysteresis: instead of strict ops/sec cap, use a sliding-window target that allows short burst reclaim when mempool free bytes < threshold. This will reduce long tail build-up but keep overall eviction rate bounded.
B) Epoch reconciliation pass: a light-weight background task triggered when per-stream deferred-free > X that attempts to reconcile stream epochs and call cudaFreeAsync or mempool API trim operations on safe synchronization points.
C) Opportunistic async flush: when allocation fallback is observed, trigger an emergency async free flush and schedule a low-cost GC pass on a background CPU thread to avoid exacerbating latency.
D) MemPool tuning: experimentally reduce arena size for short-lived allocation class and enable tighter coalescing of same-size blocks to reduce fragmentation.

Acceptance criteria / success metrics:
- Reproducer run with mitigations shows >= 70% reduction in mempool fallback events and > 50% reduction in token p99 latent spikes over baseline.
- No increase in steady-state CPU overhead > 5% and no regression in throughput.

Rollout plan:
- Prototype A,B locally, evaluate in canary pool (dedicated small hosts), collect metrics for 24h. If stable, gate into canary rollout with traffic shadowing for 48h then ramp.

Notes on trade-offs:
- Aggressive eviction reduces fragmentation but can increase write amplification and CPU utilization; hysteresis approach aims to balance.
- Forcing cudaFreeAsync on streams risks synchronization stalls if implemented naively; reconciliation must target windows where KV cache has quiesced for the keyset impacted.

Related artifacts:
See attachments for reproducer harness, perf runs, and initial prototype branch.

Added metric instrumentation for per-stream deferred free queues.

2026-03-05 Liam O'Connor: Built a small repro that narrows the trigger to mixed-length requests and high KV churn. Created branch runtime/evict-hysteresis-proto (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2892).

2026-03-06 Performance team: Reviewed baseline traces. Suggested adding sampling of cudaMemPool API calls and collecting stream epoch IDs to validate epoch drift hypothesis. Added dashboard panel request (GRAF-6121).

2026-03-08 Maya Chen: Pushed initial prototype of eviction hysteresis (WIP) and an epoch reconciliation task that posts a mempool trim on reconciliation points. Running canary on 6 small hosts now. Early signal: deferred_free counts drop but CPU increased ~8% under synthetic load.
2026-03-10 Security review (note): no customer PII in reproducer; change only memory reclamation paths, not data flows. Security team requested brief code audit before canary ramp.

2026-03-12 Liam O'Connor: Updated prototype to add safety guard to reconciliation pass so it only runs when stream has been idle for N ms. This reduced the CPU carry by half in nightly run. Preparing PR for in-repo review.
